title: Hormone feedback: glucose, calcium, water and stress
blurb: Predict which hormone the body releases when glucose, calcium or water balance drifts, and how the stress hormones take over in an emergency.
question: A nursing applicant skips breakfast before a stressful exam on a hot day and drinks nothing. Which hormones will her body release to keep her blood glucose and water balance steady, and which glands release them?

teach.h: Negative feedback runs the endocrine system
teach.body: Formally, negative feedback is a control loop in which a receptor detects a change, a control center compares it with a set point, and an effector produces a response that reverses the change. In plain English: it works like a thermostat, switching heating on when the room is cold and off when it warms up. Most hormone levels are controlled this way. Positive feedback is the rare opposite: it amplifies a change until an end event, such as oxytocin strengthening labor contractions until birth.

teach.loop: High T3/T4 inhibits TRH and TSH
teach.caption: When T3 and T4 are high, they switch off their own upstream signals: a classic negative feedback loop.
Note the parathyroids on the back of the thyroid: they raise blood calcium, while calcitonin from the thyroid lowers it.
Insulin and glucagon are antagonistic hormones. Cortisol, epinephrine and GH also raise blood glucose.
Activated vitamin D (calcitriol) helps the gut absorb calcium.
Alcohol inhibits ADH, so urine output rises. Aldosterone (Na+ retention, water follows) raises blood volume; ANP from the heart does the opposite.

teach.body: Sofia skips breakfast before her HESI A2. As her blood glucose dips, alpha cells release glucagon, and her liver breaks down glycogen. Walking into the test center, her sympathetic system triggers epinephrine from the adrenal medulla: heart racing, glucose up. The room is hot and she has not had a drink, so her plasma osmolality rises, her hypothalamus signals ADH release and her urine becomes concentrated. After lunch, rising glucose triggers insulin from beta cells, and the balance swings back.

teach.text: Reversals the HESI A2 loves: insulin LOWERS glucose and glucagon RAISES it. Glucagon is a hormone; glycogen is the stored sugar. PTH RAISES calcium and calcitonin LOWERS it. ADH DECREASES urine output. Childbirth is positive feedback; temperature and glucose control are negative feedback.

items: Negative feedback reverses a change (receptor, control center, effector); positive feedback amplifies it (oxytocin in labor).
Thyroid axis: TRH, then TSH, then T3/T4, which inhibit TRH and TSH.
High glucose: insulin from beta cells lowers it. Low glucose: glucagon from alpha cells raises it.
Low Ca²⁺: PTH from the parathyroids raises it. High Ca²⁺: calcitonin from the thyroid lowers it.
Dehydration: osmoreceptors trigger ADH, so the collecting ducts reabsorb water. Stress: epinephrine (short-term), cortisol (long-term).

summary: You can now trace the negative feedback loops that control thyroid hormone, blood glucose, blood calcium and water balance, naming the trigger, gland, hormone and effect for each. You can also separate the short-term epinephrine response to stress from the long-term cortisol response.

A.q: Thirty minutes after a large meal, a student's blood glucose rises well above its set point. Which response restores it?
A.why: High glucose triggers beta cells in the pancreatic islets to release insulin, which moves glucose into cells and into glycogen stores.

whyNot.0: Glucagon from alpha cells raises glucose, which would worsen the problem.
whyNot.2: Beta cells make insulin, not glucagon.
whyNot.3: Alpha cells make glucagon, not insulin.

A.q: A low blood calcium level directly triggers the release of which hormone?
A.why: Low blood Ca²⁺ triggers PTH from the parathyroid glands, which raises calcium back toward its set point.

whyNot.1: Calcitonin is released when calcium is HIGH, and it lowers calcium.
whyNot.2: Aldosterone controls Na⁺ and K⁺, not calcium.
whyNot.3: Thyroxine (T4) raises metabolic rate; it is not released in response to calcium.

A.q: Which of these is an example of positive feedback?
options: Insulin lowering a high blood glucose
Shivering to raise a low body temperature
PTH raising a low blood calcium level
A.why: In labor, oxytocin strengthens contractions, which trigger more oxytocin: the change is amplified until birth, which is positive feedback.

whyNot.0: Insulin reverses a rise in glucose, which is negative feedback.
whyNot.1: Shivering reverses a fall in temperature, which is negative feedback.
whyNot.2: PTH reverses a fall in calcium, which is negative feedback.

B.q: Which process does glucagon stimulate in the liver?
options: Moving glucose into muscle and fat cells
B.why: Glucagon triggers glycogenolysis (breaking glycogen down to glucose) and gluconeogenesis, raising blood glucose.

whyNot.0: Building glycogen (glycogenesis) is an insulin action.
whyNot.1: Moving glucose into muscle and fat cells is an insulin action.
whyNot.3: Glucagon is a hormone made by alpha cells; the stored form of glucose is glycogen.

B.q: A patient's blood levels of T3 and T4 are high. What is the most direct feedback effect?
B.why: High T3/T4 inhibit the hypothalamus (TRH) and anterior pituitary (TSH), a negative feedback loop that lowers thyroid output.

whyNot.1: More TRH and TSH would push T3/T4 even higher; feedback works the other way.
whyNot.2: CRH and ACTH belong to the cortisol axis, not the thyroid axis.
whyNot.3: PTH and calcitonin regulate calcium and are not controlled by T3/T4 feedback.

B.q: How does calcitonin lower blood calcium?
options: By stimulating osteoclasts to release bone calcium
By promoting calcium deposition in bone
By activating vitamin D so the gut absorbs calcium
By increasing calcium reabsorption in the kidneys
B.why: Calcitonin from the thyroid's C cells promotes calcium deposition in bone and reduces osteoclast activity.

whyNot.0: Stimulating osteoclasts releases calcium into the blood: that is PTH.
whyNot.2: Activating vitamin D increases calcium absorption, which is a PTH action that raises calcium.
whyNot.3: Increasing kidney reabsorption keeps calcium in the blood, which is a PTH action.

C.q: Devon runs a long race on a hot day and drinks nothing. Which sequence best describes his body's response?
options: Osmolality rises, ADH falls, urine becomes dilute
Osmolality falls, ADH rises, urine becomes concentrated
Osmolality rises, aldosterone falls, urine output rises
Osmolality rises, ADH rises, urine becomes concentrated
C.why: Water loss raises plasma osmolality, hypothalamic osmoreceptors trigger ADH release, and the collecting ducts reabsorb water, producing concentrated urine.

whyNot.0: ADH rises, not falls, when the blood is too concentrated.
whyNot.1: Losing water makes the blood more concentrated, so osmolality rises.
whyNot.2: Dehydration does not lower aldosterone or raise urine output; the body conserves water.

C.q: During months of caring for a sick parent, Lauren is under long-term stress. Which hormone and gland region mainly drive this long-term response, and what happens to her blood glucose?
options: Epinephrine from the adrenal medulla; raises it
Cortisol from the adrenal medulla; raises it
Cortisol from the adrenal cortex; raises it
Cortisol from the adrenal cortex; lowers it
C.why: Cortisol from the adrenal cortex drives the long-term stress response and raises blood glucose by gluconeogenesis.

whyNot.0: Epinephrine from the medulla drives the short-term (fight-or-flight) response, not the long-term one.
whyNot.1: Cortisol is made by the adrenal cortex, not the medulla.
whyNot.3: Cortisol raises blood glucose; it does not lower it.

C.q: A 52-year-old with obesity has high blood glucose even though his pancreas still secretes normal amounts of insulin. Which condition best fits?
options: Type 1 diabetes: loss of beta cells
C.why: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is insulin resistance (plus relative deficiency) and is linked to obesity and inactivity.

whyNot.1: In type 1, autoimmune destruction of beta cells means little or no insulin, but this patient secretes insulin.
whyNot.2: Diabetes insipidus is about water balance and ADH, not blood glucose.
whyNot.3: Insulin resistance is the mechanism of type 2, not type 1.

reteach.title: A thermostat and a seesaw
reteach.question: Think of a home thermostat and a playground seesaw with a child on each end. How do they explain hormone feedback?

blocks.body: A thermostat senses the room (receptor), compares it with the setting (control center) and switches the furnace (effector) on or off: negative feedback. Many hormone pairs work like a seesaw with a child at each end. When blood glucose climbs, insulin pushes it down; when it drops, glucagon pushes it up. Calcium has its own seesaw: PTH lifts it and calcitonin lowers it. The goal is always to keep the seesaw level at the set point.

blocks.text: Glucagon and glycogen sound alike: glucaGON is the hormone that makes the GLUCOSE GO up; glycogen is the stored sugar it breaks down.

explain.body: A receptor detects a change, a control center compares it with the set point and an effector responds. Negative feedback reverses the change; positive feedback amplifies it.

test.q: In a negative feedback loop, which component produces the response that reverses the change?
test.why: The effector (a muscle or gland) carries out the response that brings the variable back toward the set point.

whyNot.0: The receptor detects the change; it does not respond to it.
whyNot.1: The control center compares the change with the set point and signals the effector.
whyNot.3: The set point is the target value, not a structure that responds.

explain.body: High glucose: beta cells release insulin; cells take up glucose and the liver stores glycogen. Low glucose: alpha cells release glucagon; the liver breaks down glycogen and makes new glucose.

test.q: Insulin and glucagon are described as antagonistic hormones because they:
options: are made by the same islet cells
test.why: Antagonistic hormones have opposite effects: insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it.

whyNot.0: They come from different islet cells: insulin from beta cells, glucagon from alpha cells.
whyNot.2: Insulin lowers blood glucose; only glucagon of the pair raises it.
whyNot.3: Each binds its own receptor; antagonism here refers to opposite effects.

explain.body: Low Ca²⁺: PTH from the parathyroids releases bone calcium, makes the kidneys keep calcium and activates vitamin D for gut absorption. High Ca²⁺: calcitonin from the thyroid promotes bone deposition.

test.q: Parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium by acting on which set of targets?
test.why: PTH releases calcium from bone, makes the kidneys keep calcium, and activates vitamin D so the intestine absorbs more.

whyNot.0: PTH does not act on the liver or pancreas to raise calcium.
whyNot.1: The thyroid makes calcitonin; PTH does not act through the thyroid or skin.
whyNot.2: Muscle and liver are not PTH's calcium-raising targets.

explain.body: Rising osmolality triggers ADH, so the collecting ducts reabsorb water and urine shrinks; alcohol inhibits ADH. Short-term stress uses epinephrine from the adrenal medulla; long-term stress uses cortisol from the adrenal cortex.

test.q: Alcohol inhibits ADH release. How does this change a person's urine?
test.why: With less ADH, the collecting ducts reabsorb less water, so more dilute urine is produced.

whyNot.0: Small, concentrated urine is the effect of HIGH ADH.
whyNot.2: Extra water in the urine dilutes it, so it cannot become more concentrated.
whyNot.3: Less water reabsorption increases urine volume rather than reducing it.
